verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, on 'the doe of the dawn'. A psalm of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the singers, to be sung to the tune they call The Doe of the Dawn — a psalm of David.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is stage direction, not speech. Before the cry begins, the psalm is handed to the temple's choirmaster as a piece for performance: it was sung, not merely prayed in private. Nobody agrees what 'the doe of the dawn' is. Rashi lists a musical instrument and, alternatively, Israel as the lover-doe of Proverbs and the Song of Songs (and the rabbis read it of Esther). Radak adds a reading of the morning star, which the rabbis call 'ayyalta', and Meiri a rising instrument that starts low and brightens like the light after sunrise. Metzudat Zion says only that it was a known instrument. Ibn Ezra thinks it the opening words of a love song, a tune-title like our 'to the air of…'. Malbim hears the poem itself: dark through the first seventeen verses, dawn after. Stage it as a tune and a hint of first light.

The KJV leaves it as an unexplained 'Aijeleth Shahar' and numbers this heading as verse 0, so its 'verse 1' is the Hebrew's verse 2. Every KJV number in this psalm is one behind the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'the doe of the dawn'. Taken as a tune name, an instrument, the morning star, or an epithet of Israel; Ibn Ezra objects to deriving 'ayyelet' from the 'strength' root of 'eyaluti' in v. 20 (Heb.) because that word has no dagesh in the yod.
'To the one who leads / the choirmaster'; the root has the sense of excelling or presiding, hence the person in charge of the performance.

verses.translation_literal: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Far from my deliverance, the words of my roaring.
verses.translation_dramatic: My God. My God. Why have you left me — left me here, far from any rescue, far from the words that tear out of me like a lion's roar?
verses.directors_commentary:
Open with the doubled cry, spoken from the gut, not recited. Radak notes that Hebrew speakers double a name when calling in distress, as Elijah does on Carmel ('Answer me, YHWH, answer me', 1 Kings 18:37), as God does at 'Abraham, Abraham' and 'Moses, Moses'. The doubling is also the sound of someone who has called many times before.

'Forsaken' is the key verb, 'azav', to leave behind or abandon, used of a husband leaving a wife and of a people leaving God. The KJV, ASV, YLT all keep 'forsaken'; BBE softens to 'turned away'. The second half is a famously broken line: 'far from my deliverance, the words of my roaring', with no verb. KJV supplies 'why art thou so far from helping me' and turns the noun phrase into a second complaint; ASV, Webster do the same. The Hebrew just hangs the two nouns together, and Ibn Ezra reads it as an unfinished thought: 'my God, [you are] far from my salvation — these are the words of my roaring'. 'She'agah' is the roar of a lion or the groan of a sick man (Job 3:24), not a polite 'complaint'; KJV 'roaring' is right and ASV 'groaning' is milder.

philological_notes.note: 'You have left me / abandoned me'. A perfect, a done thing, with the pain of 'why' attached; Radak notes the corporate reading, with Israel speaking as one person in exile.
A roar, used of lions and of human cries of pain; the verbless line pairs it with 'far from my deliverance'. Ibn Ezra supplies 'my God' as the subject.

verses.translation_literal: My God, I call out by day, and you do not answer; and by night, and there is no silence for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My God, I call out in the daylight, and no answer comes. I call again in the dark, and still there is no quiet in me — no hour when my voice lies down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker no longer cries a question into the void, as in verse 2; now he keeps a ledger. Day and night together mean 'all the time', the whole round of the ancient day, and the verse is built to feel relentless: two lines, each with its own 'and not', each negating something different. God does not answer; the speaker does not stop. Play the second half as exhaustion, not defiance. Note the opening: אֱלֹהַי, 'my God', is a claim of relationship, and Ibn Ezra hears astonishment in it: if you are my God, how can you not answer, when I have no other god and never keep still for a moment?

The KJV (22:2) blurs the symmetry. It turns the first 'and not' into 'but' ('I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not'), which makes the line a contrast instead of a flat parallel, and it swaps the Hebrew verb 'answer' (ʿānāh) for 'hear': the sufferer is not complaining that God is deaf, but that God does not reply. It then keeps 'and' on the second line ('and in the night season, and am not silent'), so the English reads as a loose sentence where the Hebrew has two matched negations. The Hebrew דוּמִיָּה is a noun, 'silence, stillness', so the literal sense is 'no silence is mine'; the KJV's 'am not silent' turns the noun into a verb of the speaker's own will. Metzudat David hears it as a reasoning: a person who has been answered naturally falls silent, but not one who has not.

philological_notes.note: 'You answer': the verb for a reply, in prayer the sign that a petition has been received. The KJV's 'hearest' softens it; the complaint is silence in return, not deafness. Rashi glosses אֶקְרָא as calling 'from day to day', the answer never coming.

A noun, 'silence, stillness, rest'. Radak insists it is a noun and not an adjective, so 'there is no silence to me' is literal. Here it can mean the speaker's own silence or his lack of rest; both readings are old.

verses.translation_literal: And you are holy, sitting [enthroned on] the praises of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet you are holy. You, who sit throned upon the praises of Israel, as a king sits on his chair of state.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn begins with 'and you', a hinge, not a 'but': the whole psalm rests on the fact that the God who is silent now is the same one the nation has always praised. 'Holy' (qadosh) means set apart, other; the cry of verses 2 and 3 thus takes place under the weight of his otherness.

The second half is the verse's real difficulty. Literally: 'sitting [on/among] the praises of Israel'. The KJV's 'that inhabitest' and ASV's 'inhabitest' make 'sit' a dwelling; BBE's 'seated among' makes him a presence in the crowd; YLT's 'Sitting — the Praise of Israel' reads praise as his title. 'Yoshev' also means 'enthroned' elsewhere, hence my bracketed 'enthroned'. Rashi: he sits to hear Israel's praises from ancient days. Radak and Metzudat David: 'sit' means endure forever, as in 'You, LORD, sit forever' (Lam 5:19), so the argument is that his power now is what it was when he saved. Ibn Ezra offers the temple, the ark, 'the house of our holiness and beauty where our fathers praised you'. Direct this as a calm, almost formal line; the actor is steadying himself against the pain of the previous verse.

philological_notes.note: 'Sitting', 'dwelling' or 'enthroned'; Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'endures forever', citing Lamentations 5:19.
'Praises'; the same root gives the Hebrew name of the whole Psalter, Tehillim. Radak: praise is given after rescue, so Israel's praises are the record of past salvations.

verses.translation_literal: In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them.
verses.translation_dramatic: In you our fathers put their trust. They trusted — and you lifted them clear.
verses.directors_commentary:
A memory told like a creed. The speaker steps back from his own pain and recites the family story in a plain voice. 'Our fathers' is the line of ancestors, and the triple repetition of 'trusted' (batach, here twice) is deliberate: Radak says the repetition strengthens the claim, and that they trusted in no one else.

Trust (batach) is a physical word, to lean the weight of the body on something, which is why the verse is felt as a rescue from falling. 'Palat' (deliver) is to slip someone out of danger; the verb is rare and has the feel of a narrow escape. The KJV's 'thou didst deliver them' translates the final verb correctly as past tense; YLT turns it into a present, 'Thou dost deliver', which breaks the contrast with the present silence. The consonantal form 'vatefalitemo', with the old suffix -mo meaning 'them', is poetic and archaic; the KJV style masks it. The ancient hearer would have heard the Exodus and the wilderness behind 'our fathers'.

philological_notes.note: 'They trusted'; to rely with the weight of the body on a support. Repeated for emphasis (Radak: no trust in anyone else).
'And you delivered them'; Piel of 'palat', with the archaic pronoun suffix -mo for 'them'.

verses.translation_literal: To you they cried out and were delivered; in you they trusted and were not ashamed.
verses.translation_dramatic: To you they cried — and they escaped. In you they trusted — and they never had to hang their heads.
verses.directors_commentary:
The creed continues with a perfect balance: cry then rescue, trust then no shame. 'Za'aq' is the public cry of the wronged, the word used for Israel's cry in Egypt; 'nimlatu' (they slipped away, escaped) is the passive partner, they were delivered by another. Ibn Ezra and Radak both read 'to you' as 'to you alone, not to other gods'. That is a quiet polemic against the gods of the neighbors, and a reminder that cries in the ancient world were addressed to a named power.

The final word is the heart of the verse: 'bosh', to be ashamed or put to shame. In a culture built on honour, to trust someone and be abandoned was public humiliation. The KJV's 'were not confounded' is archaic: 'confounded' means 'put to shame', as ASV's 'not put to shame' makes clear. YLT, with 'not ashamed', is closest. This sets up verse 7, where the speaker will be exactly what the fathers were not: ashamed, mocked.

philological_notes.note: 'They were ashamed'; shame here is social exposure, a trust that is publicly disappointed. KJV 'confounded' is an archaism for 'shamed'.

verses.translation_literal: And I [am] a worm and not a man, a reproach of humankind and despised of a people.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I — I am a worm, not a man. The thing people point at to shame their neighbor; the thing a whole crowd despises.
verses.directors_commentary:
The great reversal: the previous two verses are all 'they … you', and now the word for 'I', 'anokhi', lands hard. The speaker places himself under the creed he has just recited, and he does not belong to it.

'Worm' (tola'at) was the lowest of creatures, the grub that crawls in the dust and is trodden on; 'and not a man' (ish) denies him even the standing of a person. Metzudat David reads it as weakness, 'my strength is feeble as a worm's'. Radak and Meiri read it as national: Israel in exile, scorned among the nations. Rashi too: all Israel speaks as one man. The KJV 'a reproach of men' has the plural but the Hebrew has 'adam', humankind in general, set against 'am', a people, in the second line: first all people individually, then peoples collectively. The KJV's 'despised of the people' (agent: 'of' meaning 'by') is correct but will mislead a modern ear that reads 'of the people' as 'belonging to'. BBE's 'cursed by men' is too strong and misreads the word 'cherpah', which is reproach or taunt, not a curse. Play it quiet, even flat; the violence is in the contrast.

philological_notes.note: 'Worm, grub'; also the name of the crimson dye taken from a scale-insect. Here it means something low and crushed.
'Reproach, taunt'; being a byword. KJV 'reproach' is accurate; BBE 'cursed' overstates.

verses.translation_literal: All who see me mock at me; they make a separation with the lip, they shake the head.
verses.translation_dramatic: Everyone who looks at me laughs. They split their lips in scorn; they wag their heads.
verses.directors_commentary:
A street scene: the crowd, the pointing, the lips drawn back, the heads wagging. Stage it with gesture, not with a speech; the speech comes in the next verse.

'Yafziru bsafah', literally 'they make a separation with the lip', is the odd phrase. 'Patar' is to open or release, as in 'the first-born that opens the womb' (Exodus 13:12) and 'one who lets out water' (Proverbs 17:14), which Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all cite. So the lip is opened or loosed in a sneer, and the KJV's 'shoot out the lip' (a stuck-out lip, a sneer) is a decent English guess, but literally the verb means to open or let go, not to push out. Ibn Ezra notes the preposition 'in the lip' is a rhetorical flourish and that a word may have dropped out. 'Shaking the head' is the ancient gesture of scorn, not of refusal: it appears in Lamentations and Job. Both KJV and ASV carry on with 'saying,' where the Hebrew continues straight into the next verse with no verb of speaking; the quote is implied.

philological_notes.note: 'They open, they release'; used of letting go of the womb and of water. Here, the lips opened in scorn. KJV 'shoot out' guesses at the gesture.
'They mock'. Ibn Ezra observes that this root is always joined to the preposition lamed ('to me').

verses.translation_literal: Roll [it] to YHWH! Let him rescue him, let him deliver him, for he delights in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Roll it onto the LORD!" they sneer. "Let him rescue him. Let him pull him out — he does so love this one, doesn't he?"
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the mockers' speech from verse 8, and it has no word for 'saying': the quotation begins without warning, as a jeer does. The verb גֹּל is an imperative, 'roll!', the same picture as 'roll your burden onto the LORD': hand your load to God, the way a man rolls a stone off himself. In the mouths of the scoffers it is sarcasm: you trusted him, so roll it over to him, and let him do the rescuing. The last clause, 'for he delights in him', is the cruelest line in the verse, because a delighted-in person ought not to be sitting in the dirt.

The KJV flattens all of this into narration: 'He trusted on the Lord that he would deliver him'. That puts a past tense and an indirect clause where the Hebrew has a command and two jussives, and it hides that these are the enemies' words rather than the psalmist's. The KJV is following one of the old readings in which גֹּל is not an imperative at all: Ibn Ezra takes it as an adjectival noun on the pattern of 'warm bread' (לחם חם), one who rolls his ways onto God, and compares Ps 37:5 'roll your way upon the LORD'. Radak, who reads it the same way, and Meiri compare 1 Sam 21:7 (לחם חם) and Prov 10:29 for such adjectives. Rashi takes it as an infinitive: a person ought to roll his burden onto his Maker. On any reading the effect is the same: they are quoting the vocabulary of trust back at the one who used it.

philological_notes.note: 'Roll!' The vowels allow an imperative, an infinitive or an adjectival noun. As an imperative it is the sneer of the mockers; as a noun it describes the man who rolls his ways onto God. Ibn Ezra quotes Ps 37:5; Radak and Meiri compare the adjective forms in 1 Sam 21:7 and Prov 10:29.

'He delights in him': the verb of pleasure and favour. Ibn Ezra warns that the Scripture does not make it the man who delights in God; Radak offers the other possibility, with Ps 91:14, that the man desires God.

verses.translation_literal: For you are the one drawing me forth from the belly, making me trust on the breasts of my mother.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it was you who drew me out of the womb. You who taught me to trust while I lay at my mother's breast.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now he answers the mockers, and the register drops: from the street to the birthing room. The birth is described as God's action, in the language of a midwife.

'Gochi' comes from a verb meaning to burst or break forth, used of a river bursting its channel (Job 40:23, which Rashi cites; Ezekiel 32:2, cited by Radak and Metzudat Zion). So the picture is of God pulling the baby out of the water of the womb, not the gentle 'took me out' of KJV. The participles are a present tense of character: 'you are the one drawing me forth'. 'Mavtichi' (making me trust) is the causative of 'batach', and the KJV's 'didst make me hope' softens trust to hope; ASV and YLT say 'trust'. The chain is clear: the same verb as in verses 5 and 6, now applied to a nursing baby. A baby cannot choose to trust; God put it in him. Radak: no baby feeds itself, and God makes it grow bit by bit. In ancient society a nursing mother and a midwife were the whole of survival; here those are claimed for God. 'Shadei' is plain 'breasts', a bodily word, not 'bosom'.

philological_notes.note: 'The one bringing me forth, bursting me out'; from a root used of a river bursting forth. Rashi: 'bringer-out, drawer'.
'Making me trust'; causative of the same root as 'they trusted' in v. 5-6. KJV 'hope' dulls the link.

verses.translation_literal: On you I was thrown from the womb; from the belly of my mother you [have been] my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Onto you I was thrown, from the very first hour, out of the womb. From my mother's belly onward you have been my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a double claim in a parallel pair: 'from the womb' and 'from the belly of my mother'. The speaker was hurled onto God the way a newborn is laid at someone's feet at the moment of birth. 'Hushlakhti' is passive, 'I was thrown': he did not choose. Radak reads it as the father and mother throwing their burden on God because the child cannot. The KJV's 'cast upon thee' is exact and fine here; BBE's 'in your hands' tames the verb. Rashi cites Isaiah 46:3 ('borne from the belly') for the tribes carried by God since birth.

The last words, 'my God you', put the possessive first: 'my God [are] you', the same 'Eli' that opened the psalm in the cry of verse 2. The psalm now answers its own cry: the word that began in abandonment is claimed back as a birthright. The KJV's 'thou art my God from my mother's belly' flattens the emphasis; ASV 'since my mother bare me' turns the womb into a date. Say it slowly, as an argument, not a boast.

philological_notes.note: 'I was thrown', the passive (Hophal) of the verb 'to throw, cast'. The birth is imagined as a throwing of the child onto God's lap.

verses.translation_literal: Do not be far from me, for trouble is near, for there is no helper.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not stand far from me. Trouble is close — close at my back — and there is no one, no one at all, to help.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer proper begins, after eleven verses of complaint and memory. Malbim: here the petition starts. The petition answers the opening charge point for point: verse 2 said 'far from my deliverance' and now the request is 'do not be far'. The same root, 'rachaq', frames the whole first section.

The verse is built on two 'for' (ki) clauses stacked as reasons: trouble is near, and no one else can help. Ibn Ezra notes the wordplay of 'far' and 'near' as a poetic device; Radak and Meiri read it as 'if you come near, trouble will be far'. Malbim gives the logic: a helper may stay away if the trouble is far or if another helper exists; here neither is true. 'Tzarah' is not abstract 'trouble': it is narrowness, a tight space, the sensation of being cornered. The KJV's 'trouble' is thin; 'distress' or 'narrowness' is closer. And 'ein ozer' (there is no helper) is flat: the Hebrew names the role, 'one who helps', not a person. KJV's 'there is none to help' is fine. Speak this verse quickly and low.

philological_notes.note: 'Trouble, distress'; from a root meaning 'to bind, be narrow'. The sense is of being hemmed in.
'Be far'; the same root as 'rachoq' in v. 2, so the petition is the exact reversal of the complaint.

verses.translation_literal: They have surrounded me, many bulls; mighty [bulls] of Bashan have encircled me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bulls. They are all around me, a great crowd of bulls, the heavy-shouldered giants of Bashan. They stand in a ring and the ring is closing. I can feel the heat of their breath.
verses.directors_commentary:
Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous pasture land, and its cattle were the fattest and strongest an Israelite could imagine (Radak and Metzudat Zion say exactly this; Amos 4:1 calls the wealthy women of Samaria 'cows of Bashan'). So these are not scrawny animals but the best-fed, most dangerous ones, and the speaker is on foot in the middle of the herd. Say 'bulls' with respect and a little disbelief.

KJV 'strong bulls' hides the Hebrew: the second line has no noun at all, only 'mighty ones of Bashan' (abbirei Bashan), and English must supply 'bulls' (hence the brackets). The two verbs 'surround' and 'encircle' close the line like a noose; KJV varies them as 'compassed' and 'beset me round', which is the same pair. The sound of it matters: sevavuni at the start and kitteruni at the end give the verse a ring shape. Kitteruni comes from keter, 'crown', so the circle sits at head height, like a crown (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak).

philological_notes.note: 'Mighty ones of Bashan', a poetic word for bulls (the word also names the bull in other poetry). Rashi says it is also a word for bulls fattened in Bashan; the Hebrew has no 'bulls' in this line, so the noun is supplied from the previous line.
From keter, 'crown': to surround as a crown surrounds the head. Radak adds Judges 20:43, 'they encircled Benjamin'.

verses.translation_literal: They have opened wide their mouth against me, a lion tearing and roaring.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their mouths gape open against me — wide, wet, hungry — a lion at the kill, tearing, and then the roar.
verses.directors_commentary:
The bulls of verse 13 now become predators: the metaphor turns mid-flight from herd to lion, and the verse gives us no 'like'. The Hebrew sets 'a lion' down beside 'their mouth' with nothing between them, and the commentators supply the missing comparison: Ibn Ezra and Radak both say a kaf, 'as', has dropped from אַרְיֵה, and Radak compares Gen 49:9 and 49:14, where Judah and Issachar are likewise named as animals without a 'like'. Keep that bareness when you play it. The KJV's 'as a ravening and a roaring lion' fills in the comparison and swaps the two participles for an archaism: 'ravening' for טֹרֵף, which is simply 'tearing'. BBE's 'I saw their mouths wide open, like lions crying after food' adds a seeing the Hebrew does not have and turns one lion into several.

The order, tear and then roar, matters. Radak, citing Amos 3:4, points out that a lion roars after it has killed, as a cry of triumph: the enemies first devour and then exult. Ibn Ezra's phrase 'ופצתה האדמה' links the verb פָּצוּ ('open wide') to Num 16:30, where the earth opens its mouth to swallow Korah's company, so a gaping mouth here is the mouth that swallows whole. Rashi, citing b. Megillah 11a, names the lion as Nebuchadnezzar; the psalm itself names no one.

philological_notes.note: 'They opened wide' the mouth: the verb of a jaw or a chasm, not an ordinary opening. Ibn Ezra glosses it as פתחו, 'they opened', and compares the earth that 'opens' in Num 16:30 (ופצתה האדמה). The KJV's 'gaped' is accurate but archaic.
'A lion tearing and roaring', two participles with no 'like'. Radak and Ibn Ezra say a kaf of comparison has dropped. The order is the lion's: it tears, then it roars (Radak on Amos 3:4).

verses.translation_literal: Like water I have been poured out, and all my bones have come apart; my heart has become like wax, it has melted in the midst of my inward parts.
verses.translation_dramatic: I am poured out like water, spilled on the ground, and nobody can gather me. My bones come loose, every one of them. My heart has gone soft as wax, melting, melting, down into the dark of my belly.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the body giving way. Nothing here is a wound; it is a collapse. Water that is poured out cannot be collected again (Ibn Ezra), and the speaker feels himself spreading into the dust. Radak points out that bones are harder than water, which is why the poet says they 'come apart' at their joints. Play it as weakness, not pain: the legs go first.

KJV 'my bones are out of joint' is the right idea, but it makes it sound like an injury, as if a torturer did it; Hebrew has a reflexive verb, 'they separate themselves', and no one is doing it. 'Bowels' is old English for the inner organs, and the Hebrew me'ai means the same (Radak: all the inner parts). The heart here is the seat of courage and will, so a melting heart is lost nerve, not a medical condition. Wax (donag) melts at the slightest heat (Rashi, Radak), a good picture in a land where candles and seals were made from it.

philological_notes.note: Reflexive: 'they separated themselves', not 'were put out of joint'. Radak: bones are tied one to the next, and here they come untied.
Beeswax, a substance that softens in warmth. The same simile appears in Ps 68 (Metzudat Zion).

verses.translation_literal: My strength has dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue is made to cling to my jaws; and to the dust of death you set me.
verses.translation_dramatic: What strength I had is baked dry, a broken pot left out in the sun. My tongue is stuck to the roof of my mouth, and I cannot even call. And you, you lay me down in the dust of death.
verses.directors_commentary:
From water to clay: the speaker goes from having too much liquid to none. A potsherd (cheres) is a fragment of fired pottery, the driest and most useless thing in an ancient household, and was used for scratching notes and as a scrap for ashes. The tongue that sticks to the 'jaws' is the dry mouth of fear and thirst (Rashi: when a man is in distress there is no spit in his mouth).

The last clause is the sting, and it is addressed straight to God: 'you set me'. KJV 'thou hast brought me into the dust of death' is fair, but the verb tishpeteni is an unusual one, the root used for setting a pot on the fire (shefot ha-sir, Ezekiel 24:3, Rashi and Ibn Ezra). The picture is of a pot placed on the hearth: 'you set me' there, in the dust of the grave. Say the 'you' with the voice of someone who still believes God is in charge, which is what makes the line a complaint and a prayer at once.

KJV 'cleaveth' is archaic for 'sticks'. YLT ends the verse at 'jaws' and carries 'dust of death' to the next line; Hebrew verse 16 includes it.

philological_notes.note: A dual form, the two sides of the mouth where the food is 'taken' in chewing: jaws or gums. Rashi, quoting Menachem, also offers 'my tongs'. Radak, Metzudat Zion and Meiri give the 'jaws' reading; Job 29:10 has the same picture of a tongue cleaving to the palate.

'You set me, you place me'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra connect it to the setting of a pot (shefot ha-sir), and Radak adds a midrashic picture of a pot standing at a crossroads where passers-by set pots on it.

verses.translation_literal: For dogs have surrounded me, a company of evildoers have encircled me; like a lion [are] my hands and my feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now dogs. Dogs all around me, a pack, a gang of the wicked circling closer. And at my hands and my feet, the lion again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice is now quieter and meaner. Dogs in the ancient Near East were not pets but scavengers that ran in packs outside the settlement, eating whatever was dead or weak, and calling a man a dog was an insult. Here the dogs are people, 'a company of evildoers', so the speaker is hemmed in by a crowd of small hunters and no longer by great bulls (Ibn Ezra: less than the bulls and more annoying). The KJV's 'the assembly of the wicked' is a fair rendering of 'adat mere'im, 'a company of evildoers'.

The last line is the most disputed in the psalm. The Hebrew as the Masoretes copied it says ka'ari yadai ve-raglai, 'like a lion, my hands and my feet', with no verb at all. It does not say 'they pierced', which is the KJV's reading and follows the ancient Greek translation. The Hebrew text as it stands has to supply something, and Rashi does: as if my hands and feet were crushed in a lion's mouth, citing Isaiah 38:13. Radak and Meiri take it as a lion's circle: it traps prey, and they pull in their hands and feet and cannot run. For the stage, play the helplessness; the lion bites or traps, and the rest is for the audience to hear.

philological_notes.note: 'Like a lion', one word. The sentence has no verb. 'They pierced' (KJV) rests on a different reading or an ancient translation; the Masoretic text, and every medieval commentary in the packet, takes 'lion' as the word. Rashi says the hands and feet are as if crushed in a lion's mouth; Radak and Meiri say they are held still, as prey is by a lion's circle.
'A company of evildoers'. 'Edah is the word for any gathered company, and also for Israel's 'congregation'; here it is the gang of the wicked, set against the 'assembly' (qahal) of v. 23.

verses.translation_literal: I can count all my bones; they look, they gaze at me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I could count every bone I have. And they watch. They stand there and watch me.
verses.directors_commentary:
A very quiet verse after so much noise. The speaker is thin and stripped, and the crowd does not strike him; it stares. Metzudat David says the bones stand out so much that he can count them, and that his enemies look at him with scorn. Rashi's reading is harsher: they are glad at my downfall. The verb pair 'they look, they see' (yabbitu yir'u) is doubled for the weight of the staring. The preposition is 'on me', which in Hebrew can mean a look of satisfaction (compare Ezekiel 28:17 'they look on you', Radak's example).

The KJV 'I may tell all my bones' uses 'tell' in its old sense of 'count' (compare 'bank teller'), which a modern reader reads wrongly. Its 'they look and stare upon me' is a faithful rendering of the two Hebrew verbs. Radak and Meiri mention a second reading in which 'atzmotai' means 'my strong arguments' and the speaker is telling his case to the great men, who only look on him with contempt; I keep the plain reading of bones.

philological_notes.note: 'I count' (piel), the same root as 'book' and 'recount' (cf. v. 23, asapperah shimkha, 'I will recount your name'). Ibn Ezra links the two verses: the speaker counts his bones now and will count God's name later.
Two verbs of looking set side by side. Rashi hears glee; Metzudat David hears scorn.

verses.translation_literal: They divide my garments to themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.
verses.translation_dramatic: They share out my clothes between them. Over my robe they throw the lot, to see who takes it home.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is being stripped of everything he owns, and the crowd is treating him as already dead. In the ancient world a person's clothes were among his main possessions: a garment was cloth that took weeks to weave, and a good robe could be a family's wealth, and the cloak was the poor man's only blanket and security for a debt. Dividing someone's garments is dividing the estate of the dead or the plunder of the beaten, and casting lots (goral, a small stone or marker, thrown or drawn) settles who gets the piece that cannot be cut.

There is no parallel with a later event in the Hebrew, and I leave that to the reader. What the text says is a single line: 'they distribute my garments to themselves, and on my clothing they cause a lot to fall'. The line is a pair: 'garments' (begadai) and 'clothing' (levushi) are two words for the same thing, a parallelism, and Metzudat David says exactly that: the saying is doubled. Malbim reads levushi as the royal or specially fine garment, and Ibn Ezra takes it as a hint that the speaker is a king.

KJV 'vesture' is archaic for 'clothing', and 'part' for 'divide'. 'Cast lots' is plural in KJV; the Hebrew has the singular 'a lot', the verb being 'make fall'.

philological_notes.note: 'They make a lot fall', in the singular. The lot was a small marker thrown or drawn to decide the matter; the verb is causative of 'fall'.
Two words for clothing in parallel. Metzudat David: the matter is doubled. Malbim and Ibn Ezra hear in the second a royal or special garment.

verses.translation_literal: But you, YHWH, do not be far; my strength, hurry to my help.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD, do not stay far from me. You are my strength. Come to help me, come quickly.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn. After all the images of the crowd, the speaker says 'and you', with a pronoun placed first in the Hebrew (ve'attah), which makes the contrast sharp: they, and you. He returns to the plea he made in v. 12, 'do not be far', and now the words are shorter and more urgent. The verb is a jussive, 'may you not be distant', a plea and not a statement. Let the actor stop describing and speak straight to God.

The KJV has 'O Lord' for the four letters YHWH, which hides the name God gives himself. 'My strength' is the rare word eyaluti, found only here in the Bible; it comes from a root for strength (Rashi compares Ps 88:5, 'a man without strength'), and it is a title and a name for God at once: 'my strength'. Ibn Ezra says do not wonder how David can call God this, for God is his strength. The KJV 'haste thee to help me' is good but archaic; the Hebrew 'chushah' is a bare imperative, 'hurry'.

philological_notes.note: A rare word, 'my strength'. Rashi connects it with 'ayal' in Ps 88:5 and Gen 31:29 ('it is in the power of my hand'); Metzudat Zion gives the same sense. It is a name for God as the strength of the speaker.

verses.translation_literal: Deliver my life from the sword, from the hand of the dog my only one.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pull my life away from the sword. Take my one life out of the dog's paw.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the pleas go in the order of the dangers. Ibn Ezra says the sword answers the company of evildoers and the dog answers the dogs of v. 17. The sword is the one new weapon, a real one, and it shows that the danger is not only an image. The sword (cherev) is a feminine noun in Hebrew, one of the ordinary weapons of any soldier.

The last word is the one every English version softens. Yechidati is 'my only one', from yachid, 'single, only'. Here it names the speaker's life or soul as the one thing he has left and cannot replace (Malbim: the one thing that remains after they have taken all else; Metzudat Zion and Radak: the soul, unique among the body's parts). KJV 'my darling' is a poor guess, a word from the age of Shakespeare for 'a dear one', which fits the sound but not the root; BBE 'my life' loses the 'only'. Note too that 'hand of the dog' is literally 'hand', which YLT turns into 'paw'; the Hebrew is the ordinary word for hand, the same used for human power, so a dog with a hand is a person.

philological_notes.note: 'My only one': in parallel with 'my life' (nafshi), the one life he has. Medieval commentators read it as the soul, which is single and unlike any other part of a person; Malbim reads it as the last thing left to him.
'From the hand of a dog': 'hand' is the usual word for power. Metzudat David reads the dog as a person who bites like a dog; Radak reads it as a nation among whom Israel is in exile.

verses.translation_literal: Save me from the mouth of a lion, and from the horns of wild oxen you have answered me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Save me from the lion's mouth. And from the horns of the wild oxen, you have answered me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The plea runs through the animals again: lion (from v. 14), now the wild ox, whose horns replace the bulls of v. 13. In a single line the speaker moves from a command, 'save me', to a plain statement in the past, 'you have answered me', with no particle between them. Nothing in the Hebrew explains the jump, and it is the turning point of the whole psalm. Ibn Ezra reads the answer as past kindness, 'you have already done a mercy for me from such a trouble', and Metzudat David the same: you have always answered me before. Play it as the moment the voice changes: the same man, a different breath.

KJV 'unicorns' is a famous mistake. The Hebrew re'emim are wild oxen (the aurochs, a huge horned wild bovine now extinct), the animals of strength; the Greek translators rendered the word as 'one-horned', and the English followed it. The horns are plural in Hebrew (the dual 'qarnei'), and Ibn Ezra reports that the wild ox was thought to be the strongest of horned beasts. YLT's 'high places' reads the word as ramim, 'heights', which the text of the verse does not need. KJV 'hast heard' for 'anitani' is a reasonable sense of 'answered'.

philological_notes.note: Wild oxen (aurochs); the aleph is dropped in this spelling, as Ibn Ezra notes. The beast is famous for its horns (Deut 33:17, cited by Radak). KJV 'unicorns' comes from the Greek, not from the Hebrew.

'You have answered me', a perfect after an imperative. Radak and Meiri give two readings: 'answer me' as a prophetic perfect, or a statement of past rescues. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'you have already done me this kindness'.

verses.translation_literal: I will recount your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will praise you.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will tell your name to my brothers. In the middle of the gathered people, I will praise you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood of the whole psalm changes here. The man who was surrounded and counting his bones is now standing in the middle of a crowd of his own people, and the crowd is friendly. Say the first line gently and the second one openly: 'brothers' are the close circle, and the 'assembly' (qahal) is the public meeting of the people, where a rescued person tells what happened. Ibn Ezra reads 'my brothers' as the men of my confidence, and Metzudat David reads the line as 'then I will tell the miracle publicly'.

The verb in line one is the one he used for counting his bones: 'asapper' there, 'asapperah' here (Ibn Ezra links them). First the speaker counts his own bones for scorn; now he counts out (recounts) God's name for praise. KJV 'declare' hides that the verb is the one used for counting, and 'congregation' is KJV's habitual word for qahal, with a church sound. The form of both verbs is a first person with the added -ah, a cohortative, a resolve ('let me tell'), and the English 'will' covers it.

The assembly (qahal) here is also the opposite of the 'company' (edah) of evildoers in v. 17: one gang closes in on him, another gathers to hear him.

philological_notes.note: Cohortative of 'to count, to recount'. Ibn Ezra sets it against 'asapper' in v. 18: the speaker who counted his bones now counts God's name.
A public assembly of the people, the place where praise is spoken aloud and a rescue is made known. Metzudat David: then I will tell the miracle in public.

verses.translation_literal: You who fear YHWH, praise him; all the offspring of Jacob, honour him; and be afraid of him, all the offspring of Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: You who fear the LORD, praise him! All you children of Jacob, honour him! And tremble before him, all you children of Israel!
verses.directors_commentary:
This is what the speaker says to the assembly: the praise itself (Ibn Ezra on the previous verse). It is a call in three beats, to three groups, with three verbs: praise, honour, be afraid. Let it build and open out, so the actor becomes a leader of song. The groups widen: first 'those who fear YHWH', then 'the offspring of Jacob', then 'the offspring of Israel'. Radak says this is how a psalm lists in Psalm 135, 'house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, you who fear YHWH', each according to his rank and nearness, and the midrash he quotes reads 'fearers' as converts or as priests. Ibn Ezra takes the 'fearers' to be those of the other nations.

The pair 'Jacob' and 'Israel' are the same man under his two names, and the poem uses them as parallel words for the whole people. The last verb is the surprise: guru, from a root meaning 'to dread' (Rashi: language of fear; Metzudat Zion: they are afraid), not 'to sojourn', which has the same consonants. The KJV keeps 'fear him', which is accurate but repeats its own 'ye that fear the Lord' and so blurs the shift; the ASV's 'stand in awe of him' softens the verb to reverence, and YLT's 'be afraid' is closest. 'Fear' in the first line is the ordinary religious word for reverence, but this last verb is real trembling. The speaker's own terror of the lions has turned into the proper fear of God.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who fear YHWH', a group of the faithful. Ibn Ezra: they are those of the nations; Radak: they are of Israel, one rank among several, like the lists in Psalm 135; the midrash he cites reads them as converts or as priests.
From a root meaning 'to dread', a different word from the verb 'to sojourn'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion both gloss it as fear.

verses.translation_literal: For not he-despised and-not he-detested the-affliction-of an-afflicted-one, and-not he-hid his-face from-him, and-in-his-crying-for-help to-him he-heard.
verses.translation_dramatic: He did not look down on the suffering of the sufferer. He did not turn from it in disgust. He did not hide his face. When the poor man cried out, he heard, and the cry did not go unanswered.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns here. Until now the speaker has been the one whose God hid, did not answer and stood far off (verses 2–3, 12, 20). Now he says the opposite of each complaint, and the actor should let the old fear still show in the voice: 'he did not hide his face' answers 'why have you forsaken me' point for point. Face-hiding is the vocabulary of covenant anger and of a patron who will not receive a petitioner. In a world where a poor man had no standing before a king or a judge, the claim that the God of the universe attends to the cry of the powerless is the whole point.

The Hebrew plays on one root: 'the affliction of an afflicted one' (ענות עני), as if to say the suffering belongs to the sufferer and God takes it as his own concern. The KJV does carry 'affliction of the afflicted', but it stiffens the verbs ('hath despised', 'abhorred', 'hath hid') into archaic perfects, and 'abhorred' is softer than שקץ, which is the word for ritually detestable things (Leviticus 11:11–13); God does not treat the sufferer as if he were unclean. The last clause is the quiet climax: three negatives, then one plain positive, 'he heard'.

philological_notes.note: 'The affliction of an afflicted one': a repeated root, with the second word naming the person and the first his condition. Rashi takes ענות as 'cry' and, alternatively, as 'submission' (as in Exodus 10:3); Ibn Ezra takes it from עני.
'Detested': used elsewhere for creatures and things that make a person ritually repulsive. God does not treat the afflicted man as repulsive.
'Hid his face': the idiom for withdrawn favour and attention. It answers the psalm's opening complaint of abandonment.

token_glosses.gloss: and in his crying for help

verses.translation_literal: From-with-you [is] my-praise in-[the]-assembly great; my-vows I-will-pay before those-fearing-him.
verses.translation_dramatic: My song of praise comes from you, and I will sing it in the great assembly. The vows I made in my trouble I will keep, before all who fear him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from describing to addressing God ('from you'), then slips back to 'him' in the same breath. That swing between 'you' and 'he' is typical of Hebrew prayer and should be played as a man too moved to hold a steady grammatical person. The point of 'from with you' is that even the praise is a gift: the rescue is what gives him something to say. The great assembly (קהל רב) is the pilgrim crowd at the sanctuary, and the vows are the promises made in the crisis. In the world of the psalms a vow made in distress was paid with a thank-offering and a shared meal, with the whole community watching, so that the rescue became public knowledge.

The KJV 'My praise shall be of thee' is correct but vague, and it makes the verb a future, where the Hebrew has no verb at all; ASV 'Of thee cometh my praise' is nearer. 'Them that fear him' is an old-style phrase for those who worship the LORD.

philological_notes.note: A verbless clause: 'from with you [is] my praise'. Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all read it as 'you are the cause of my praise', because you rescued me.
'I will pay my vows': payment language. Malbim identifies the paying as the thank-offering brought for a deliverance.

verses.translation_literal: They-will-eat [the] humble and-be-satisfied; they-will-praise YHWH, those-seeking-him; may-live your-heart for-ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: The humble will eat, and eat until they are full. Those who seek the LORD will praise him. And may your hearts live, live for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a feast, and it should sound like one. Hunger is the background: the poor have known empty stomachs, and 'be satisfied' (שבע) is the word for being fed to the full. Metzudat David and Malbim tie the meal to the thank-offering of the previous verse, whose meat was eaten by the worshippers and the poor invited to share (see Leviticus 7:15); that is my reading too, since the verse itself does not name a sacrifice. The speaker is now host, pouring out the rescue as food.

Then comes a sudden turn to the second person plural: 'your heart'. The speaker leans toward the crowd and blesses them. The verb is a jussive, a wish, not a promise: 'may it live'. The KJV 'your heart shall live for ever' turns a blessing into a prediction; ASV 'Let your heart live' is right. 'Heart' (לבב) is the seat of courage and vitality. Ibn Ezra and Radak link 'live' to Jacob's spirit reviving on hearing that Joseph was alive (Genesis 45:27), and set it against Nabal, whose heart 'died within him' (1 Samuel 25:37). KJV 'the meek' for ענוים flattens a word that also means the poor, the bowed, those pushed low.

philological_notes.note: 'The humble, the poor': the same root as 'afflicted' in verse 25. Those who were afflicted are now those who eat.
A jussive blessing, 'may your heart live'. Radak connects it to Genesis 45:27, where the heart revives, and contrasts it with 1 Samuel 25:37 where a heart dies.

verses.translation_literal: They will remember and they will turn to YHWH, all the ends of the earth; and they will bow down before you, all the clans of the nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will remember, and they will turn back to the LORD, all the far ends of the earth. And before you they will bow down, every clan of every nation.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera pulls back from a single banquet table to the whole map. The psalmist has been praising in Jerusalem; now he sees the furthest edges of the known world coming home. The 'ends of the earth' were the limits of what an ancient Israelite could picture: far coasts, deserts and mountain lands. 'Remember' (zakhar) has to carry weight: they will recall what they had forgotten, which is what makes the turning a return (shuv) and not a conversion in the modern sense. The verse moves from 'to YHWH' to 'before you' in mid-sentence; the speaker again drops from description into address.

The KJV has 'the ends of the world' for 'eretz', which means 'earth' or 'land'; 'kindreds' is archaic for 'clans'; and 'worship' translates the verb for prostration (hishtachavot), literally 'to bend low'. A performer should physically feel the bowing. Nations in the ancient Near East bowed to a king as an act of submission, which prepares the next verse about kingship.

philological_notes.note: 'Ends of the earth': the farthest edges. Ibn Ezra notes that even those at the edge will remember and turn when they hear of the wonder.

'And they will turn to YHWH': the verb of repentance and return. Rashi reads 'they will remember' with an object: the nations will remember the evil that befell Israel when they see Israel's good fortune, and then turn to YHWH. Radak and Meiri likewise have them remember Israel's low estate or their own, and see the deliverance.
Prostration, not merely 'worship': a full bow to the ground, the gesture owed to a king.

verses.translation_literal: For to-YHWH [belongs] the-kingship, and-[he is]-ruling among-the-nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the kingship belongs to the LORD. He rules over the nations.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason for everything before it, introduced by 'for' (כי). It is short on purpose. Say it plainly and slowly, as a declaration, not a hope. Within a psalm of an afflicted individual, the claim that God is king of the whole world is audacious, and it is what makes the helpless man's cry worth hearing: the one who hears him is also the one who rules the powers that crush him.

The KJV 'the kingdom is the Lord's' is fair, but מלוכה is more abstract, 'kingship' or royal rule, the office more than the territory. 'Governor' for the participle מושל is a little cold and bureaucratic. The Hebrew is simply 'he is ruling'. In an age in which every nation had its own king and its own national god, the line asserts that the real kingship belongs to Israel's God alone, whose rule does not stop at any border. Radak and Meiri tie it to Zechariah 14:9, 'the LORD shall be king over all the earth'.

philological_notes.note: 'The kingship': royal rule as an abstract right, with the article, so 'the' kingship, the true one.
A participle: 'ruling', as an ongoing state, which is why 'is ruling' is better than a bare noun. Radak connects it to Zechariah 14:9.

verses.translation_literal: They ate and they bowed down, all [the] fat ones of [the] earth; before him will kneel all [those] going down [to the] dust, and his soul he has not kept alive.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have eaten, and they bow down, every one of the fat and well-fed of the earth. Before him they will kneel, all who go down to the dust, and no man among them has kept his own soul alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a table laid for the whole earth, and then as a floor everyone ends up on. The 'fat ones of the earth' (dishnei-eretz) are the well-fed, the rich and prosperous. After the poor man's meal in verse 27, 'the humble shall eat and be satisfied', here the prosperous eat too, and then bow. Notice the sharp mirror: the fat sit at the bottom of the scale as well, 'those who go down to the dust', the dead or the dying. Two ends of a life, both on their knees.

The verbs are the problem. The Hebrew has a perfect ('they have eaten') followed by a vav-consecutive ('and they bowed down'), then an imperfect ('will kneel'). The KJV smooths it into 'shall eat and worship' and quietly turns the fat into a subject who 'worships', which is a pleasant, harmonized picture. It also rewrites the last clause as 'none can keep alive his own soul', which supplies a modal 'can' the Hebrew does not have: the text says only that he 'has not kept his soul alive', with a singular verb and a singular 'his' after a plural subject. Actors must hear that jolt, a sudden single man in the crowd.

The tradition splits on who these people are. Rashi reads the clause 'they ate and bowed' as an inverted sentence, the humble eat the fat of the earth and bow to the LORD; and he reads the dead of the wicked in Gehenna as kneeling without mercy. Ibn Ezra takes the fat ones as those who luxuriate in this world and, at the end of their days, bow to the king who gathers their spirit, with no power to rebel. Radak, in his father's name, gives a second reading: the 'descenders to dust' are the ones who killed Israel, who go down to Gehenna, and God will give life to none of them (citing Joel 4:21, 'I will not acquit their blood'). Malbim reads the fat ones as men who fatten their bodies like stall-fed calves and neglect the soul. Choose one for the scene and do not play all of them.

philological_notes.note: 'The fat ones of the earth': the adjective dashen means fat, rich, well-nourished. It is a rare word; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as from dashen, 'fat, oil'. In a psalm about the poor (ענוים, verse 27), the rich are those who at first did not need God. Rashi reverses the logic and reads the 'fat' as the abundance the humble eat.

'Those going down to the dust': a participle, so those in the act of descending: the dying, or the dead already in the grave. Metzudat David takes it as people destined to go down into the dust of the grave; Meiri takes it as Sheol, the lowest place.

'And his soul he has not kept alive': the verb chiyah is a piel perfect, 'to keep alive, to give life to', with 'his soul' as its object; the subject is not stated. Rashi takes it as 'does not make alive', God not reviving their souls; Ibn Ezra and Malbim take it as the man who cannot keep himself alive.

verses.translation_literal: Offspring will-serve-him; it-will-be-recounted of-[the]-Lord to-the-generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: A people yet to come will serve him. The Lord will be told of, generation after generation.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the dust the psalm turns back to life, and forward. 'Offspring' (זרע, literally seed) is the next generation, the children who will keep faith when those speaking are gone. The actor should lighten the voice: the weight of the dying has passed, and the story is handed to the young.

The verse is grammatically compact and the KJV, 'it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation', is nearly unreadable. The verb ספר in the passive intensive stem means 'be recounted, told', not 'be reckoned', so ASV 'it shall be told of the Lord unto the next generation' is closer. The Hebrew is bare: 'it will be recounted to [the] Lord to the generation'. The preposition ל before 'Lord' can mean 'about', so the Lord is the subject of the telling. Rashi reads the clause as reordered ('the next generation will be told, to the praise of the LORD, what he did'); Ibn Ezra reads 'the generation' as the generation to come. Malbim reads it as 'counted in the number of generations', and the Targum identifies the seed as Abraham's. All the readings agree that faith is handed down by telling.

philological_notes.note: 'Seed, offspring': a collective singular, the descendants. Rashi and Radak identify them as the seed of Israel; the Targum as the seed of Abraham.
A passive intensive of 'to count, tell': 'it will be recounted'. The KJV 'accounted' hears the counting sense; most others hear the telling.

verses.translation_literal: They-will-come and-they-will-declare his-righteousness to-a-people being-born, that he-has-acted.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will come and tell of his righteousness to a people not yet born: he has done it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a verb without an object. 'He has acted' (עשה). It does not say what; after twenty-one verses of abandonment, mockery, dogs, thirst and dust, the speaker no longer needs to say what. The entire psalm is the missing object. Let the last two words land as a quiet, flat statement of fact, not a shout.

The KJV supplies 'this' ('that he hath done this'), and the ASV 'it'. The brackets are fair, but they close a gap the Hebrew leaves open. 'Righteousness' (צדקה) in the psalms is not courtroom justice but God's saving, putting-right action, what he does for the afflicted. The speakers 'come' to a new generation, a 'people being born', which echoes the 'seed' of the previous verse. Ibn Ezra reads the 'people born' as the third generation, and Meiri as the children after them, to whom the miracles are retold. Note also Radak's long note at this verse, an anti-Christian polemic about readings of this psalm; I leave it aside as irrelevant to the word-by-word sense here.

philological_notes.note: 'His righteousness': his saving justice, the deeds by which he sets things right for his people.
'A people being born': a participle, a people of the future. The Targum renders 'a people that is destined to be born'.
'That he has acted': no object. Metzudat David fills it 'what he did with them'; I leave it open.
